v.why: Raising a very small learning rate fixes underfitting within 243 epochs (exps 1, 2, 17), giving large gains compared with elsewhere.
At already-large learning rates, a further increase makes Adam training diverge (exps 5, 9, 19, 20).
Lowering an unstable, too-large learning rate recovers trainability, a much larger benefit than lowering a moderate one.
Increasing an already-strong L2 penalty causes heavy underfitting (exps 45, 57-60), while small alphas are harmless to raise (41-43).
With tiny batches the L2 penalty is applied far more often per epoch, so raising alpha hurts much more (exps 52, 54 vs 53, 55).
Deeper nets are less stable at large learning rates, so adding a layer there collapses accuracy (exps 84, 85, 94).
At small learning rates the extra layer adds capacity and speeds fitting without instability (exps 83, 86, 93).
Small batches give noisy gradients and many updates, so a larger learning rate destabilizes training more (exp 9 vs 10) and helps less at low learning rates (exp 18 vs 17).
Larger batches reduce gradient noise and damp the instability caused by high learning rates (exps 28, 31).
With a tiny learning rate, fewer updates per epoch from bigger batches worsen underfitting (exps 26, 30).

raw:
Here are 10 interaction hypotheses supported by the 100 single-seed experiments:

- **Learning rate dominates.** Raising it helps a lot from the bottom of the grid (experiments 1, 2, 17) and is catastrophic at the top (5, 9, 19).
- **Effects depend on learning rate.** Depth and batch-size edits change sign depending on whether learning rate is low or high (83, 86 vs 84, 85; 30 vs 31).
- **Weight decay is only harmful when already large.** Raising the L2 penalty barely matters at small values but hurts at large ones (44, 45, 57–60), and much more with tiny batches (52, 54 vs 53, 55).
- **Small batches make high learning rates worse** (9 vs 10).
